Dada

The printed graphic work of Dada (about 1916–1924): magazines, posters, broadsides, and invitations in Zürich, Berlin, Hannover, Cologne, Paris, and New York. Pages mix many unrelated typefaces, sizes, and angles from the jobbing printer’s case, and Berlin artists cut press photographs into photomontage. The movement also covers readymades, assemblage, sound poetry, and performance. This record covers its typographic collage and photomontage and treats the other branches as related work.

Irreverent / Chaotic / Ironic / Experimental / Rebellious / Raw

Visual grammar

  • Mixed cases. One page or one line combines heavy grotesques, high-contrast romans, condensed gothics, and ornaments from the jobbing printer’s case. Sizes jump from caption to poster scale inside a line.
  • Lines at several angles. Lines of type run at different angles, upside down, or vertical on one page. There is no shared grid or axis. Blocks overlap and crowd each other.
  • Photomontage. Photographs cut from the illustrated press, with heads, machines, crowds, and words pasted together. The cut edges are visible, and the scale of the pieces does not agree.
  • Black on newsprint, sometimes one red. Most work is printed in black on cheap paper. Red is the usual second color. The grey of the halftone photograph is the third tone.
  • Printer’s material as image. Rules, brackets, pointing hands, stock blocks, and ticket fragments become compositional elements, not only dividers.
  • Flat printed paper. Letterpress and line block on paper, with pasted pieces in original collages. No gloss, gradient, or soft shadow.

Identity

Name
Established movement name
Also called
Dadaism, Dada typography, Dada photomontage
Era
1916–1924. From the Cabaret Voltaire in Zürich (1916) to the move of Paris Dada into Surrealism (about 1924). Schwitters continued Merz typography into the 1930s.
Regions
Switzerland, Germany, France, United States, Netherlands

Name used by
Wikipedia: Dada (sections “Photomontage” and “Circulation”), Getty AAT: Dada (300021500), Wikidata: Dada (Q6034), Tate: Art term “Dada”, Tate: Art term “Photomontage”, Wikipedia: Kurt Schwitters (Merz periodical and typography)

Lineage

  • Influenced by Cubism. Wikidata lists Cubism as an influence (P737). Cubist papier collé is the usual source given for Dada collage.
  • Influenced by Futurism. Wikipedia says Dada developed in the context of the Futurist movement. Futurist parole in libertà had already freed type from the line.
  • Influenced by Expressionism. Wikidata lists Expressionism as an influence (P737). Wikipedia names it, with Cubism and Futurism, among the movements Dada emerged from.
  • Related to Constructivism. Wikipedia says El Lissitzky edited and typeset Schwitters’s Merz 8/9 (1924), and the Bauhaus record notes that Moholy-Nagy brought constructivist photomontage to the school. Both movements use photomontage, so late Dada and early Constructivist print overlap.
  • Related to De Stijl. Wikipedia says Theo van Doesburg wrote Dada poetry as I.K. Bonset and published the Dutch Dada magazine Mécano (1922–23).
  • Related to Surrealism. Wikipedia says the energies of Paris Dada merged into Surrealism by the mid-1920s. Tate says the Surrealists later adopted photomontage.
  • Related to Grunge typography. The grunge record cites Eskilson’s Graphic Design: A New History for the influence of Dada on 1990s illegible typography.
  • Related to Pop art. The Pop art record cites the Getty AAT scope note that Pop art was influenced by Dada.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Three or more unrelated typefaces appear in one composition, often in one line.
  • Lines of type run at several different angles, with no shared grid.
  • Cut photographic fragments are combined with type, and their edges stay visible.
  • Black on paper dominates, with at most one strong second color, usually red.
  • Printer’s ornaments such as pointing hands, rules, or brackets are used as images.

Rules it out

  • One typeface family set on a consistent grid.
  • Gradients, gloss, soft shadows, or rounded components.
  • Torn, eroded, or blurred letterforms. Dada letters are clean metal type; the disorder is in the arrangement.
  • A palette of several bright hues.

Often confused with

Constructivism
Both use photomontage and red and black on paper. Constructivism builds an ordered, directed composition with one heavy sans-serif in capitals, diagonal bars, and wedges. Dada mixes unrelated faces at random angles and sizes, with no geometric system. Some late pieces, such as Merz 8/9, sit between the two.
Grunge typography
Grunge also collides many faces, but its letters are damaged, blurred, and digitally layered over dirty texture. Dada letters are clean metal type on plain newsprint, and its texture is the halftone of the photographs.
New Wave typography
New Wave stays inside one grotesque family and works with letterspacing, stepped lines, and dot screens. Dada mixes serif, grotesque, and ornament faces and uses press photographs.
Pop art
Pop art uses comic-strip images, Ben-Day dots, and several flat bright hues. Dada uses press photographs, mostly black and one red, and no comic devices.
Punk visual art
Punk ransom-note flyers revive Dada collage with photocopies and cut-out letters glued by hand, often with dirt and toner. Dada used letterpress and line blocks, so its type is clean.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Set the page in black on a warm newsprint color. Use red as the only strong hue.
  • Use at least three unrelated typefaces: a heavy grotesque, a high-contrast roman, and a condensed gothic. Change face, size, and case inside one heading.
  • Rotate headings, labels, and pasted slips to several different small angles.
  • Use black-and-white photographs cut to irregular straight-edged shapes, and paste type labels on them.
  • Use printer’s ornaments such as the pointing hand (☞), heavy rules, and brackets as visual elements.
  • Keep body text in a plain readable roman, so the collage stays in headings, labels, and images.

Keep the function

  • Do not erode, blur, or distress the letterforms. The disorder comes from arrangement, not from damaged type.
  • Do not use gradients, rounded corners, or soft shadows.
  • Do not add more than one strong hue beyond black and paper grey.
  • Do not align everything to one grid. A tidy collage loses the style.
  • Do not rotate or overlap body text or form controls so that they become hard to read or use.

Useful directions: art and performance events, experimental music and club nights, independent magazines and zines, satirical or protest campaigns, gallery and exhibition sites.

Poor fits:

  • Banking, healthcare, and government services. The style mocks authority and order, which these services need to show.
  • Dense data apps and long reading. Mixed faces and angles slow scanning.
  • Children’s products. The source tone is satirical and anti-bourgeois, not playful.
